description: This topic teaches learners how texts are organised and how to condense them, covering sequence words, the 5Ws and 1H method, paraphrasing, retelling, reordering jumbled sentences, and completing partial stories logically.

mcq.questionText: Which word is commonly used to show the FIRST event in a sequence of actions?
mcq.explanation: "First" is the sequence word that signals the very beginning of a set of actions. Exam Tip: learn the common sequence words in order: first, then, next, after that, later, finally.

mcq.questionText: Which word is commonly used to show the LAST event in a sequence of actions?
mcq.explanation: "Finally" signals the last or concluding event in a sequence. Exam Tip: "finally" almost always appears near the end of a well-organised passage.

mcq.questionText: Read: "Juma woke up early. First, he washed his face. Then, he ate breakfast. Finally, he went to school." What is the SECOND event in this passage?
mcq.explanation: The events occur in this order: waking up (1st), washing his face marked by "first" (2nd), eating breakfast marked by "then" (3rd), and going to school marked by "finally" (4th). Exam Tip: match each sequence word to the event it introduces before numbering the events.

mcq.questionText: A summary of a story should:

options.text: Include every single detail from the original
Include only the main ideas, expressed briefly in your own words
Be longer than the original text

mcq.explanation: A summary condenses a text down to its essential main ideas and is written in the reader's own words. Exam Tip: a summary is always shorter than the original and never copied word-for-word.

mcq.questionText: Which method helps a reader identify the key elements of a story by asking who, what, when, where, why and how?
mcq.explanation: The "5Ws and 1H" method organises the essential elements of a story using six question words. Exam Tip: this method is widely used both for comprehension and for planning your own writing.

mcq.questionText: When retelling a story that you have read, it is important to:

options.text: Change who the main characters are
Keep the main events and details, even if the wording is different
Only mention the title of the story
Add unrelated new events that never happened

mcq.explanation: Retelling means keeping the essential events and details of the original story while allowing the wording to change. Exam Tip: retelling is not the same as inventing new events.

mcq.questionText: Read: "The dog barked loudly. Then it ran towards the gate. A stranger was standing there." Which of the following is the BEST one-sentence summary?

options.text: A dog barked and ran towards a stranger at the gate.
A stranger opened the gate quietly.

mcq.explanation: This option captures the key events and the reason for them in the fewest words. Exam Tip: a good summary answers "what really happened" using as few words as possible.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following best describes a "jumbled" text?

options.text: A story told clearly from beginning to end
Sentences of a story printed in a mixed-up order that needs to be reordered
A dictionary definition of a word
A single word written on a card

mcq.explanation: A jumbled text presents the parts of a story out of their correct order, so the reader must rearrange them. Exam Tip: look for sequence words such as first, then and finally to help you reorder a jumbled text.

mcq.questionText: Which sentence would most likely appear at the BEGINNING of a well-organised story?

options.text: Once, there was a small village near a big river.
Later, the children returned to school.

mcq.explanation: "Once, there was..." introduces the setting and characters, which is typical of a story's opening. Exam Tip: story openings usually introduce the setting before any sequence words appear.

mcq.questionText: In the 5Ws and 1H method, which question word asks about the REASON something happened?
mcq.explanation: "Why" is the question word that asks for the reason or cause of an event. Exam Tip: remember who = person, what = event, when = time, where = place, why = reason, how = manner.

mcq.questionText: When a reader paraphrases a message, they:

options.text: Express the same meaning using different words
Ignore the meaning of the message completely
Always translate it into another language

mcq.explanation: Paraphrasing means restating the same meaning of a message using different words. Exam Tip: paraphrasing is related to summarising, but it focuses on rewording rather than shortening.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following best demonstrates "reading for comprehension"?

options.text: Reading quickly without thinking about the meaning
Reading a passage and being able to explain its main ideas afterward
Reading only the title of the passage

mcq.explanation: Comprehension means truly understanding a text, which is shown by being able to explain it afterward. Exam Tip: comprehension is about understanding, not simply about reading the words.

mcq.questionText: A story completion task typically asks students to:

options.text: Continue or finish a partial story in a logical way
Translate the story into another language
Copy the story exactly with no changes

mcq.explanation: A story completion task gives students a partial story and asks them to continue it logically. Exam Tip: a good completion stays consistent with the characters, setting and tone already established.

mcq.questionText: Which technique most helps a reader understand the ORDER in which events happened in a passage?

options.text: Identifying sequence words such as first, then, after that and finally
Reading only the last sentence of the passage
Randomly guessing the order of events

mcq.explanation: Sequence words explicitly signal the order in which events take place. Exam Tip: highlighting sequence words as you read is a practical comprehension strategy.

mcq.questionText: Compared with the original text, a good summary should be:

options.text: Significantly shorter, while still keeping the main ideas
Exactly the same length as the original

mcq.explanation: A good summary condenses the text substantially while still capturing the main ideas. Exam Tip: if your "summary" is nearly as long as the original, it still contains too much detail.

fib.questionText: Words like "first", "then" and "finally", which show the order events happen in, are called ____ words.
fib.explanation: Words such as first, then and finally that show the order of events are called sequence words. Exam Tip: sequence words are the quickest clue to the order of events in a passage.

fib.questionText: A brief statement of the main ideas of a text, written in one's own words, is called a ____.
fib.explanation: A short restatement of the main ideas of a text in the reader's own words is called a summary. Exam Tip: a summary must always be shorter than the original text.

fib.questionText: The method that uses the question words who, what, when, where, why and how is called the ____ method.
fib.explanation: The six question words who, what, when, where, why and how together make up the 5Ws and 1H method. Exam Tip: use this method to plan a summary or check that you understood a passage fully.

fib.questionText: Restating a message using different words while keeping the same meaning is called ____.
fib.explanation: Restating a message in different words while preserving its meaning is called paraphrasing. Exam Tip: paraphrasing changes the wording, not the meaning.

fib.questionText: A text with sentences mixed up that a reader must put back in the correct order is called a ____ text.
fib.explanation: A text whose sentences have been mixed up and must be reordered is called a jumbled text. Exam Tip: find the sentence without a sequence word first, since it is usually the opening.

fib.questionText: Retelling a story means repeating the main events even if the exact ____ used is different.
fib.explanation: Retelling keeps the main events of a story even when the exact wording changes. Exam Tip: never change the characters, setting or ending when retelling a story.

fib.questionText: The ability to understand and explain a text's meaning after reading it is called reading ____.
fib.explanation: Understanding and being able to explain what a text means after reading it is called reading comprehension. Exam Tip: being able to retell or summarise a passage is proof of comprehension.

fib.questionText: A task in which students continue a partial story in a logical way is called story ____.
fib.explanation: A task that asks students to continue a partial story logically is called story completion. Exam Tip: keep the same characters, setting and tone when completing a story.

fib.questionText: In the 5Ws and 1H method, the question word that asks about location is ____.
fib.explanation: "Where" is the question word in the 5Ws and 1H method that asks about the location of an event. Exam Tip: pair each question word with its purpose: who = person, where = place.

fib.questionText: A good summary is generally much ____ than the original text.
fib.explanation: A summary is generally much shorter than the original text because it keeps only the main ideas. Exam Tip: if a summary is not noticeably shorter, it has not been condensed properly.

tf.questionText: Sequence words like "first" and "finally" help readers understand the order of events.
tf.explanation: Sequence words directly signal when each event takes place in relation to the others.

tf.questionText: A good summary should be much longer than the original text.
tf.explanation: A good summary should be significantly shorter than the original while keeping the main ideas.

tf.questionText: The 5Ws and 1H method uses the question words who, what, when, where, why and how.
tf.explanation: These six question words are exactly what make up the 5Ws and 1H method.

tf.questionText: Paraphrasing means copying a text word-for-word without making any changes.
tf.explanation: Paraphrasing means expressing the same meaning using different words, not copying it exactly.

tf.questionText: A jumbled text has its sentences arranged in a mixed-up, incorrect order.
tf.explanation: By definition, a jumbled text presents sentences out of their correct order so they can be reordered.

tf.questionText: When retelling a story, it is acceptable to add completely new, unrelated events.
tf.explanation: Retelling should keep the original events; adding unrelated new events changes the story incorrectly.

tf.questionText: Reading comprehension involves understanding a text, not just decoding the words on the page.
tf.explanation: Comprehension is about grasping meaning, which goes beyond simply recognising the words.

tf.questionText: In the 5Ws and 1H method, the question word "why" asks about location.
tf.explanation: "Why" asks about the reason for an event; "where" is the question word that asks about location.

tf.questionText: Story completion tasks require the reader to continue a partial story in a logical way.
tf.explanation: This is exactly what a story completion task asks students to do.

tf.questionText: A summary should include every single detail from the original text.
tf.explanation: A summary should include only the main ideas, not every detail from the original text.

summary.correctAnswer: Words such as first, then, next, after that and finally that show the order in which events happen.
summary.explanation: Spotting these words helps a reader reconstruct the correct order of events in a passage.

summary.correctAnswer: A short statement of the main ideas of a text, written in the reader's own words.
summary.explanation: A summary is always much shorter than the original and avoids unnecessary detail.

summary.correctAnswer: A method that organises the key elements of a text using who, what, when, where, why and how.
summary.explanation: It is a practical tool for both reading comprehension and planning writing.

summary.correctAnswer: Restating the same meaning of a message using different words.
summary.explanation: Paraphrasing focuses on rewording rather than shortening a text.

summary.correctAnswer: A text whose sentences are printed in a mixed-up order and must be rearranged correctly.
summary.explanation: Sequence words are the main clue used to reorder a jumbled text.

summary.correctAnswer: Repeating the main events and details of a story, even if the exact wording is changed.
summary.explanation: Retelling must not invent new events or change the characters and setting.

summary.correctAnswer: A task in which a partial story is given and the reader must finish it logically.
summary.explanation: A good completion stays consistent with the characters, setting and tone already established.

summary.correctAnswer: The ability to understand a text and explain its meaning after reading it.
summary.explanation: Comprehension is shown through explaining, retelling or summarising a passage accurately.

summary.correctAnswer: Arranging events of a text in the correct order in which they happened.
summary.explanation: Sequencing relies on identifying sequence words and matching them to events.

summary.correctAnswer: The introduction of a story that establishes the place, time and characters before the sequence of events begins.
summary.explanation: A well-organised story usually introduces its setting before sequence words appear.

hoq.questionText: Reorder these jumbled sentences into a logical story: (i) "Finally, he thanked the old man and went home." (ii) "One day, a boy found a lost dog near the market." (iii) "Then, he searched for the dog's owner." (iv) "First, he gave the dog some water and food."

options.text: (ii), (iv), (iii), (i) — starting with the setup, then the sequence words first/then/finally mark the progression

hoq.explanation: Sentence (ii) has no sequence word and sets the scene, then (iv) "first", (iii) "then" and (i) "finally" mark the logical progression of events. Exam Tip: find the sentence without a sequence word first, since it is usually the opening, then match the remaining sequence words to their correct order.

hoq.questionText: Read the passage: "The village had experienced a long drought. Crops failed and people struggled to find food. Eventually, the government provided emergency food supplies." Using the 5Ws and 1H method, what are the "why" and the "what" of this passage?

options.text: Why: the government provided food; What: there was a drought
Why: a long drought caused crop failure and food shortage; What: the government provided emergency food supplies
Why and What refer to exactly the same information
Neither why nor what can be identified in this passage

hoq.explanation: The "why" is the underlying problem, the long drought that caused crop failure and food shortage, while the "what" is the main event or response, the government providing emergency food supplies. Exam Tip: in cause-and-effect passages, "why" usually points to the earlier problem, and "what" often points to the response that follows.

hoq.questionText: A student writes a very long "summary" that includes almost every sentence from the original text, just reworded. Why is this NOT a good summary?

options.text: This is a perfect summary because it is thorough
It is not a good summary because a summary must be significantly shorter and include only the main ideas, which the student should identify using a method such as 5Ws and 1H before writing briefly
Summaries should always be the same length as the original
The student should make the summary even longer

hoq.explanation: A genuine summary distills a text down to its essential main ideas in a much shorter form, rather than rewording nearly every sentence. Exam Tip: if your summary is close to the same length as the original, you have paraphrased the whole text rather than summarised it.
